December 9, 1969

maintopic: POSSIBLE BRITISH ENTRY INTO ECM-SAFEGUARDING OF CANADIAN INTERESTS

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONSIDERATION OF SOCIAL CREDIT MONETARY PROPOSALS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, in order to remedy the economic paralysis in Canada, parliament should give serious consideration to the monetary proposals of the Social Credit party and proceed as soon as possible with the following:
1)	financing of public funds by credit advances at a nominal cost by the Bank of Canada to be repaid at the rate of depreciation of the works achieved;
2)	distribution of a national dividend to each Canadian citizen in order to ensure, out of the Canadian national product, at least his minimum living expenses;
3)	balancing the sum of prices attached to the Canadian national product with the purchasing power in the hands of the consumers by means of a discount allowed to the latter.
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to move, on behalf of the Ralliement creditiste, the motion which appears on today's order paper and which deals first of all with the economic paralysis in Canada, and also with the measures that the Creditistes are proposing to correct the situation.
There is no need for long speeches to prove that economic paralysis does exist in Canada at the present time. As a matter of fact, it is enough to read the briefs submitted yesterday by the provincial premiers at the third constitutional conference. The latter are all agreed that it is not to constitutional problems that the conference should devote its time but rather to economic ones.
There are several types of economic problems: inflation, regional disparities, unemployment, investments, taxation and taxing powers.
Although they are different, these problems have one common aspect. They all have

financial consequences, for in order to settle all these problems we have to talk solely about money and financing.
That is the key to the solution of all these problems. Each time the provincial premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) meet at federal-provincial conferences they have to deal with the same matter, to tackle the same question: money.
When confederation was established, the provinces were given their own responsibilities, such as education and road construction. The federal government kept the responsibility for finance.
The prime responsibility of the federal government was and still is to make funds available to the provinces, so that the latter may discharge their duties adequately.
The prime responsibility of the federal government is to provide financial blood, which is money, and make it available to each of the provinces. But since it does not play its part, the provinces do not have enough funds or financial blood to discharge their responsibilities adequately. Therefore, we note that the members of the Canadian financial body, that is the provinces, increasingly wish to part from it, on account of the deficient flow of financial blood. The financial paralysis has affected each member of confederation.
More and more, each member would like to separate from the Canadian economic body which does not allow it to live because of a lack of economic blood or money. Every one accuses the government of feeding some members too well, to the prejudice of others. Lack of economic vital fluid is mostly due to a financial haemorrhage suffered by the federal government that does not allow the Bank of Canada to operate in keeping with the Canadian resources and the needs of the provinces, a financial haemorrhage which we should not tolerate.
To the eight chartered banks of the country, the federal government sold for a mess of pottage-the campaign fund-the power to manipula e, to create and to destroy the economic blood of the nation, that is credit, that only a so-called sovereign government should possess and keep, by controlling the Bank of Canada.
That is the cause of the financial haemorrhage in Canada. And that is why the provinces are paralysed and why several of them obviously want more and more to part from the body which "separates" them, because it does not supply them with the economic blood, money, that it had undertaken to provide
December 9, 1969	COMMONS
them in the early days of confederation so that each one might carry out its responsibilities.
The Cred tistes are not the only ones nor the first ones 10 note that Canada is paralysed by the sovereign power to issue and control the coun ry's currency, a power which has been used for private purposes rather than for the common good, as the government should.
I should like, at this point, to quote authorities in several fields, who said before us what we have been saying in this House for about 30 years, and who denounced the financial system which s ifles the provinces and the federal government.
The former prime minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King said in 1935, and I quote:
As soon as a nation ceases to control its currency and its credit, it does not matter who makes the laws. Usury once under control ruins all nations.
In his encyclical letter Quadragesima Anno, Pope Pius XI stated, and I quote:
This power becomes particularly irresistible when exercised by those who, because they hold and control money, are able also to govern credit, and determine its allotment, for that reason supplying so to speak, the life blood to the entire economic body, and grasping, as it were, in their hands the very soul of production, so that no one dare breathe against their will.
All economic life has become terribly hard, cruel and implacable.
Some bankers and economists have also discovered before us what we are describing today. Mr. Graham Towers, governor of the Bank of Canada, had this to say, and I quote:
Evidently, the banks create money out ol nothing.
Mr. R. G. Hawthrey, an eminent economist and a high official of the Treasury Board, stated the following, and I quote:
When a bank makes a loan, it creates money out of nothing.
Mr. Eccles, president of the United States Federal Reserve Bank said, and I quote:
Banks create and destroy money.
And Reverend Georges-Henri Levesque,
O.P. remarked:
When high finance and the two old-line parties fight Social Credit, they fight against the common people since Social Credit is for them what light is to man. They constantly persecute the supporters of Social Credit for fear of losing their monopolies and their powers.

If you want neither communism nor socialism, set Social Credit against them, for into your hands it becomes a terrible weapon against these two enemies.
I should also like to quote U.S. presidents and financiers such as, for instance, the former Canadian Finance Minister, the Honourable Donald Fleming who stated in 1959:

I emphasize that the government of Canada has no power of control whatsoever over the money supply.

And the Right Honourable Reginald McKenna stated, and I quote:

And on page 394 of the proceedings and evidence of the Committee on Banking, Trade

Question: Will you tell me why a government with power to create money should give that power away to a private monopoly, and then borrow that which Parliament can create itself, back at interest, to the point of national bankruptcy?

speechtext:
Now, if Parliament wants to change the form of operating the banking system, then certainly that is within the power of Parliament.

The Right Hon. Prime Minister Mackenzie King said on June 27th, 1934, as reported in Hansard:

As I said the other evening, once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility all talk of the sovereignty of Parliament and of democracy is idle and futile.

United States President John Adams said in 1787, and 1 quote:

All the perplexities, confusion, and distress in America arises, not from the defects of the constitution or confederation-not from want of honour or virtue so much as from down right ignorance of the nature of coin, credit and circulation.

I could cite hundreds of other statements by financiers and economists who said before us what we are repeating about the control of finance in Canada.
The explanations and the quotations I have just given justify the Ralliement Creditiste's wish to change our present financial system and to give Parliament a necessary and absolute authority as regards control over issuance of money and creation of credit.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
In my opinion, the lengthy list of authorities in that field is sufficient to convince us that it is urgent and imperative for parliament to bring about the necessary solutions to the present financial problems. To those who claim that Social Credit is wrong-which is not yet proved-I retort that the present system has already proved without any shade of doubt that it is wrong.
For example, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been talking for some time about inflation. The steps he advocates to fight it

remind me of firemen who, to fight a fire, will stir it up.
Inflation is the result of the present financial system. Creditistes are charged, often through ignorance, with wanting to establish an inflationist system in the country.
Inflation is here in Canada right now, and growing daily, and yet we do not have Social Credit. There are two potential causes for inflation: scarcity of money or scarcity of products. When products are in short supply, prices go up, but that is not our problem for the time being since there is no scarcity of products in Canada.
Scarcity of money can also be a cause of price increase, or inflation. When consumers are short of money, strikes occur; they in turn result in salary increases, which contribute to higher prices. That is the only cause for the inflation we are experiencing in 1969.
A shortage of purchasing power forces consumers to claim higher wages, which brings about price increases. Increases in salaries because of strikes, tax increases by all governments, interest rate increases at all levels, those are the three main reasons why prices get higher, thus downgrading the purchasing power. Increases in expenses for consumption are followed by a reduction in the purchasing power and by an increase in production costs.
We suggest that, to fight inflation, we must achieve an economic equilibrium between production and consumption by a well-balanced purchasing power. Our economic system is made of three elements: production, distribution and consumption.
It is proven that our wealth distribution system is wrong and inadequate since it does not permit the high modern production to reach the consumers.
It belongs to the governments to govern and if our financial system does not permit the distribution of the goods we are able to produce it should be replaced by another. Many backward economists and theoricians say that consumption should be financed by production. We, creditists, say that because of the insufficient buying power resulting from the production process, a gap is caused between the total consumption prices and the total buying power resulting from this very same production.
Under the present system, people try to close this gap by means of mortgages or debts on the future. They try to close this gap by putting into the consumers' pockets money obtained through getting into debt, so that this debt money and the money earned
December 9, 1969

through the production process, may enable the citizens to buy goods.
This is a fallacy which may be worded as follows: Buy today the production of yesterday with the money of to-morrow. Or to put it differently: Incur debts for the future generations to live today with the production of yesterday!
Adam Smith, the world-renowned economist and author of the Wealth of Nations stated in connection with the objective of production:

Consumption is the sole aim and purpose of production.

The aim of production is consumption. Our economic system is made up of three areas: production, consumption and distribution, and nobody now believes production to be lacking, because all provinces, social classes, manufacturers and sellers, at any level, are faced with the so-called problem of production and even overproduction, as we are told.
And in the meantime, all provincial governments, and every city and municipality are faced with social problems. They are a prey to misery, poverty, or the victim of regional disparities despite abundance.
Production is not lacking, yet consumption is inadequate. Two thirds of mankind have to do without the bare necessaries of life in 1969. In Canada, the problem is similar. Why? Because our distribution system of goods and services does not work, or works inadequately-
We suggest therefore that the federal government, which controls the issue of money and credit in the country, should keep in circulation an amount of money equal to the total amount of production.
In other words-and that is easy to understand-the amount of money in circulation should be based on the total amount of production. If the production in Canada is worth $72 billion in 1969, the government should maintain economic balance through the Bank of Canada by circulating $72 billion by which it is always possible to buy for $72 billion worth of the production proposed to the Canadian people.
But, under the present system, there are about $50 billion in circulation whereas the production of goods and services is worth $72 billion. One should not try to pour a gallon of
DEBATES	1751
Monetary Proposals of Social Credit Party liquid into a quart container or to put a ton of anything in a 500-pound bag or 72 gallons of gasoline into a 50-gallon container.
How then should $72 billion production be distributed with a purchasing power of $50 billion? Social Credit wants to balance the Canadian purchasing power against the global volume of production, that is to say, to base the amount of circulating currency on production. Money should serve production and production should be subordinated to consumption. Money is a medium of exchange and the money in circulation should be equal to the value of goods to be exchanged.
Does not the federal government issue as many stamps as are needed to post all the letters of this country? Stamps have a specific face value and they are issued according to postal requirements. We have nothing to say against this.
Money has also a nominal value and there should enough of it to match production. Why should there be a lack of drinking water in the house when lakes, rivers and municipal reservoirs are full, if not because the water system, that is the aqueduct is out of order or too small?
Why should one freeze in the house when the tank is full of fuel oil, if not because the heating system which distributes the heat is out of order or is not working?
Why should the worm in the apple die of hunger, if not because the apple is too big?
Why should we die of thirst in a boat on a lake, if not because we are lying tied and bound in the bottom of the boat?
At the present time, the government is tied and bound in the bottom of the financial boat and that explains the economic paralysis in Canada.
In 1935, the Prime Minister of Canada, the right hon. William Lyon MacKenzie King, promised during the election campaign to fight big finance, but once in office, he failed to do it. Once more, the capitalists won without having to fight and the people were once again deceived.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding my remarks, I would like to suggest some practical solutions to the problem of finance in Canada, as well as to the distribution of wealth. We have proposals to make to the government which unfortunately, is tied and bound in the bottom of the financial boat while people are starving even in a period of abundance.
1752	COMMONS DEBATES	December 9. 1969
Monetary Proposals of Social Credit Party The first thing I would like to deal with is the following:

(1)	Restoration to the sovereign community of effective control of money in all its forms and
(2)	The establishment by the Canadian Parliament of the machinery which would secure regular equation between the community's production and the community's purchasing power.
Social Credit supplies the principles upon which such machinery can be constructed. In brief these principles are as follows:
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The setting up of the Credit Authority, consisting of statistical experts whose duty it will be to draw up a statement of consumption and production of consumer's goods for a convenient period expressed in terms of dollars at current prices. This account would be drawn up at the end of each accounting period and would provide the measure of the extra money needed by the people to buy all the goods produced. The results of one period's production and consumption would provide the basis of the issue of extra money for the ensuing period and it follows that the extra money to equate consumption with production would in this way be based on the amount of goods produced but unsold in the earlier period.
Two methods of issuing the extra money are proposed and they are inseparable if the method is to be technically sound. This feature cannot be overemphasized. They are the dividend and the scientific price discount. Purchasing power can be increased either by increasing incomes without an increase in prices, or by lowering prices leaving incomes unchanged.
The dividend will increase incomes and in theory would be paid as a right to every member of the community although expediency might dictate that it should be used to pension the aged, give greater educational facilities or improve services in some other desirable way. The price discount would apply to all retail sales and would be a fiat rate calculated according to the figures in the hands of the Credit Accountants.
The essential point is that together the price discount and the dividend would make up the deficiency of purchasing power in the hands of the consumers.
If we take token figures and put production at 10 and consumption at 7-if the dividend distributed one unit then the price discount would be 20 per cent and thereby the whole of the gap would be made up.
If the discount were 20 per cent, all retail prices would be marked down by that rate and the retailers would be reimbursed by an issue of credit which would be debited to the Credit Account. Just like the present system of finance as has been explained, the Social Credit system would be a system of bookkeeping. The difference would be that the issue of money would be based on the amount of goods in existence and would be a true representation of the physical facts instead of one in which poverty and unemployment exist simultaneously in a rich land. The price discount is the supreme discovery of Major Douglas because it offers a means of translating into accountancy the truth that the cost of production is consumption. The physical cost of producing is the amount of energy used in

that production. That means the food, etc., consumed by the producers. The financial cost under the present system includes factors which do not represent food etc., consumed, and the books are falsified. The price discount by enabling goods to be sold below financial cost would bring the books into line with physical facts.

These explanations summed up in the motion debated today, would allow Canadians to enjoy a logical, sensible and well-balanced economic system. Production could reach the consumers, thus enabling about 100,000 families who are at present living on family allowances, to work and produce for the benefit of all Canadians.

Those theories will be defended by my friends of the Rallie-ment Creditiste. They no doubt will be attacked by members of the other parties. It is a debate we have had a good many times in this House.
However, Mr. Speaker, I welcome most strongly the motion placed before this House which suggests in paragraph (2) that a first charge on the production of this nation should be the guarantee of minimum living expenses to every Canadian. There are many ways in which to phrase that proposal, but I submit that in whatever way one puts it, it relates to the most important question facing this country, namely the absolute necessity of our abolishing povety in Canada. I agree with my hon. friends that branching out into various side issues is not the way to abolish poverty, nor will we do so by concerning ourselves with other things. We should come directly to the problem and see to it that we get the means of livelihood into the hands of all our people.
Surely, it is not necessary for us to stress the urgency of the poverty problem, but I do
December 9, 1969

have two or three press clippings or quotations that I should like to put on the record, a couple of which came into my hands a few days ago.
A press dispatch from Vienna quoted Mr. Maurice Strong, the President of the Canadian International Development Agency, who made a speech at the Vienna Development Institute in that city recently. Mr. Strong spoke about the blight of poverty as it hangs over our world and I should like to quote a couple of sentences from the report of his speech.
It is not realistic to expect the people of the less developed countries to reach the level of affluence of the developed countries in the foreseeable future, Strong said. But dire poverty forcing people to live in sub-human conditions has to be overcome.
Then, there is this direct quotation from Mr. Strong:
"Today for the first time in history this is a practical proposition. I share the conviction of those who say that if it is not done, civilized life on our planet may not survive much beyond the end of this century.
A new dark age is not a vague threat. It is a real possibility."
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
That is the world picture. Mr. Strong went to some lengths to make it clear that the gap between the rich and the poor, the gap between the have and the have-not nations, is actually growing and that it can engulf our whole civilization unless we do something about it. That clipping, incidentally, came into my hands almost at the same time as another which includes a photograph of a certain family, underneath which are these words:
Aristotle Onassis and his wife Jacqueline, the former Mrs. John Kennedy, have managed to spend between $15 and $20 million since their marriage last year. Big spender? Not really... not when you have nine residences which have a total of 202 servants on duty at all times around the world.
I shall not comment on that, Mr. Speaker; I have simply read it into the record. But I suggest that these two clippings taken together, on the one hand, poverty so harsh that it could engulf our civilization and, on the other, downright sinful affluence, present a situation about which we simply must be concerned.
Lest we think this problem is not so much domestic as it is international, I would remind hon. members again of the forthright statement made to us in the Fifth Annual Report of the
DEBATES	1753
Monetary Proposals of Social Credit Party Economic Council of Canada in that important chapter on poverty:
Poverty in Canada is real. Its numbers are not in the thousands, but the millions. There is more of it than our society can tolerate, more than our economy can afford, and far more than existing measures and efforts can cope with. Its persistence at a time when the bulk of Canadians enjoy one of the highest standards of living in the world is a disgrace.
Further on in the course of this chapter the Economic Council points out that 27 per cent of the people in the non-farm population of Canada are living below the poverty line, and that the figure is 29 per cent if one includes both farm and non-farm population. The Council does give different sets of figures, and it says that in some cases the statistics given may be a little high. But it states on page 110 of the report that to describe at least one Canadian in every five as suffering from poverty would not appear to be an exaggeration.
So, Mr. Speaker, the problem is with us; it is with us in the world, and it is with us in Canada. I do not blame the members of the Ralliement des Creditistes for giving us once again their theories. Some hon. members on the other side will probably tell us that their theories are silly-that is the word which is often applied to them. But I suggest they are not half as silly as the principles upon which we are working in this country today, the principles which leave us with a few people who enjoy great affluence while at least a fifth, and probably a quarter, of those who live in Canada endure dire and degrading poverty. We have got to cope with this issue. We have got to solve it.
It seems to me that sometime, soon, we must face the fact that there is no easy solution, no magic trick, no financial, fiscal or monetary formula which, if put on the books, will solve the problem. The fact is, we must get more goods and services, more housing, more education, more health care, more money into the possession of all our people. Therefore, when my friends on my immediate left talk about the desirability of making arrangements which would provide a guaranteed annual income for all our people I am happy to stand in this House and commend them for having brought this issue to our attention.

I am pleased that the federal government has said that it is a national, a federal responsibility, to be concerned about providing or protecting the incomes of all our people. I hope I am not misinterpreting the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) if I see it in this light. He is saying, it seems to me: We must maintain family allowances under federal control so that we can do something about the income position of the young; we must keep old age pensions under our control so that we can protect the incomes of people who have retired; for those in the in-between group, we must keep unemployment insurance under our control and we must also, as the federal government, be responsible for sickness insurance and income maintenance. So today there is talk about a guaranteed annual income. What puzzles me in the words I have heard from the Prime Minister this week, in the white paper, and in the radio and television despatches, is a line of his which goes something like this: It is our responsibility to be concerned for people, and to do something for them, when they are poor, when they are unemployed, when they are ill, when they are old, and so on.
Can we not get to the point at which we do things for people in Canada simply because they are people? It is this eternal categorizing of people as poor, as unemployed, as welfare cases, which bedevils any attempt to build a just and humane society in Canada. We have to get the means of livelihood to the people as people. This is why I welcome the language in the second part of the resolution under which a portion of our national product would be distributed to all the Canadian people simply because they are Canadians, simply because they are human beings, simply because they are here.
Most hon. members who have been around half as long as I have been here, let alone all the time, know how strongly I have felt during all my public life about means tests and incomes tests. I think they are degrading because of the reasons I have just tried to put forward; they pick out people not as human beings but as welfare statistics. The day will

come when we shall get away from that attitude and, instead, provide goods, services and money for people just because they are here, just because they are Canadians.
It is the universality of the concept in the second part of the resolution which appeals to me. I think this is a concept we shall have to adopt if there is to be any question of a just society, of a more humane society, of any kind of society with any heart in it at all. I come back to what the Prime Minister has been saying in the last few days, both in the white paper and to the federal-provincial conference. I welcome his insistence that the protection of incomes must be a federal responsibility so that there may be a sense of community among Canadians from coast to coast. I commend him for it. But my heart sinks when I hear him destroy this concept by saying, in effect, that we can only do things for people when they are old, or sick, or unemployed or otherwise disadvantaged. We do not provide education on this basis. We do not provide roads or postal services-if we still have postal services-or national defence on this basis. All these things, and many others, we provide on a universal basis. They are here for all of us.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I think that a certain standard of living for all of us must come, and that it will come. I have no doubt in my mind that it will come, even if it takes two or three decades. Therefore, it hurts me to see the Prime Minister, who poses as a progressive, a modern thinker, a swinger, talking this old language of doing things for people because they are in need. In other words, he means a means test, he means a needs test, he means a shelving of the principle of universality, which I think is the only principle upon which we can build a just society.
I know the cry will come back that this kind of a just society will cost money. I would not be surprised if this cry comes in the speech that will be made when I sit down. might have made him a human being instead of just another welfare statistic.

I think what has to happen is that we must produce all of the goods and services we can, and that we have to distribute and redistribute those goods and services on the basis that as a first priority there must be a guaranteed minimum income for all our people. If this means challenging the myth about a wage and salary elite, then I am all for it. The poor farmer may be on poorer land, but there are farmers who have less ability than others and there are men in business who have much less ability than others. This variation, I suggest, will always exist. It is one philosophy to say to everyone that because they are men or women they will be entitled to so much income or will be entitled to enjoy so many goods and services and no more because if they do produce more it will be taken away from them and given to others. That is a complete egalitarian philosophy.
But, on the other hand, I say to the Chef du Ralliement-

-to the leader of the Ralliement credi-tiste, who has been constantly preaching us in this House, that we must not tax the "haves" in favour of the "have-nots", because before long, there would only be "have-nots".

In other words, you cannot tax to transfer income from the "haves" to the "have-nots", at least in the context of the many repeated remarks of the Leader of the Social Credit Rally (Mr. Caouette). But I say to you, Mr. Speaker, in the light of the fact that we do have an insufficiency of goods and services, we must progress faster in exercising the priorities or demands of government and we must also proceed to determine the appropriate allocation of the resources. At the present time the public sector, federal, provincial and municipal, tax upwards of 37 per cent of the gross national product. It is estimated on good authority that on the basis of the actions of government at all three levels the demands of education, medicare, social welfare and other programs within the next five years will require 41 per cent of the gross national product.
It is very instructive, however, to note that in order to achieve that 4 per cent increase in the allocation of resources to the public sector it will require 45 per cent of the increase in the gross national product over the next five years. I would point out that this certainly would not be acceptable in my province, nor in any developing province, where people are prepared to work extra long hours. They are not bound by the hours of a negotiated agreement. They will work extra hours. They will absorb the worry involved in arranging for

credit, meeting payrolls or obtaining other resources by using some of the ingenuity the good Lord gave them and some of the extra courage that is given to man to produce more. That is how we increase our gross national product. That is how we develop our country. This is how this country was developed so that we are able to sit here today, in this generation, and enjoy the resources we have.

Are we to
say to a man, a woman or a particular industry-people grouped in that industry-shall be penalized by extra heavy taxation so that the fruits of their extra labour may be distributed to others? This I do not believe Canadians as a whole are prepared to accept. We do not have that acceptance of an egalitarian society.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I will say this: I recognize it is my duty morally as a citizen of this country to assist my fellow man, but I will not accept that I must provide him with three mattresses on which he may lie for the rest of his life. I will provide him with assistance and encouragement so that he can become self-reliant and can produce. But, except in the case of those who are incapable by reason of illness, infirmity or circumstances beyond their control, I would say we as Canadians believe that every penny and every dollar spent for what is called the welfare of the public must be earned by somebody. It must be earned and it must be paid over to the government. The ability to support that type of expenditure is limited. It is like a business where the owner or those in control thereof-they can be shareholders-milk much more than the profit from the business. In other words, if the owner lives off the shelf of his inventory that business will die. In the same way our economy will die if we continue to draw more than we require to maintain the level of production, to renew our production and to increase our production.
Our Canadian society will improve with respect to its cultural achievements and its social justice only on the basis that the people themselves will work to increase the base upon which we can draw for the necessary funds, the necessary energy, and the necessary personnel required to carry out what might be called public activities. But if we are going to turn everything into the government, into the public sector, where are the
December 9, 19G9

people who will work in the public sector? From where will they be drawn? From the other pools? We do not have a shelf of trained people in this country. We are underpopulated. We are under-skilled, and yet we find proposals that would make us prodigal of our resources.
I would say it is far better for us to proceed on the basis that we can preserve our economy, that we can make it expand and thereby encourage not only our own people to produce, but others to come here. It may come as a shock to hon. members to know that our birth rate has reached the point where we are barely renewing our population. We are at a point in the reproduction of our own population that is lower than the point in 1935, which was the previous low in Canadian history. Do we think we are going to develop this country and are going to have added population as a result of our own efforts? Of course not. We will have to rely on people who come to us from other lands. We will have to attract those people, and they are very good people, let me assure you. But they must be attracted to this land and opportunity provided for them. If we do not follow that course they will not come, and we will stand still.
I cannot find within the terms of the motion before us the type of encouragement that I would want for the society that I feel is required in order that we can put its resources together and develop our country. Of course, we will do things imperfectly, Mr. Speaker. My goodness gracious, we are human beings prone to error, subject to influences from outside this country over which we have no control.
I listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) talking about interest rates. Does he feel he can unilaterally drive down interest rates by government decree, particularly since the greatest influence on our interest rates comes from the United States. There is no Watkins formula that will eliminate that influence. We are social animals in this country, just like people in any other country. We cannot isolate ourselves within our own country. We live as a result of our inter-relationship with our fel-lowman in other countries. His conditions affect us; ours affect him. We are imperfect men. We make mistakes; we made them in the past and we will continue to make them in the future. But there is one thing we can do, and that is bend our energies and capabilities toward using our resources in the best possible way so that we can develop our country. I must say I cannot find any incen-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONSIDERATION OF SOCIAL CREDIT MONETARY PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us today a motion presented by the Ralliement Creditiste which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, in order to remedy the economic paralysis in Canada-
1.	Financing of public funds-
2.	Distribution of a national dividend-
3.	Balancing the sum of prices attached to the Canadian national product with the purchasing power in the hands of the consumers-
Before dealing at length with the subject, since Social Credit is a subject one can speak of at length, I should like first to point out certain remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). He referred earlier to that famous recession which we experienced from 1930 to 1940. He himself was one of those who were clothed by Canadians to go and fight for freedom on the battlefields of Europe for quite a substantial salary, following a very serious recession. In fact, the Canadian people found a way to feed those freedom fighters, to clothe them and to make it possible for them to throw bombs over Germany in the name of freedom.
Today, we experience an unacceptable inflation. One day I had a discussion with an economist and he told me that inflation is worse than the recession we experienced from 1930 to 1940. In fact, we all know that with $1 we cannot do much today.
If the hon. member for Edmonton West were intelligent, he would give intelligent explanations throughout Canada. In my opinion, this hon. member is nothing but the ombudsman of the loan sharks. He keeps on advocating a long obsolete system. In 1900, the explanation he gave would have been acceptable, for at that time Social Credit was practically unknown.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
He accuses us of always repeating that we do not want to tax the rich in order to give to the poor. But this is simply communism and we are against communism. We want some purchasing power to be made available both to the rich and to the poor so that they may all lead a comfortable life in a country as rich as ours.
He went on to say that further credit is not advisable, since it would step up the pace of evolution, thus increasing inflation.
1760	COMMONS
Monetary Proposals of Social Credit Party
I wonder whether the chartered banks, whose profits have increased by 29 per cent, now suffer from inflation? Does inflation only affect chartered banks? The hon. member for Edmonton West is anxious to keep on extending his protection to those who are reaping extravagant profits and he does not see the dire poverty now prevailing.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, in supporting the motion introduced by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), I thought of conveying to the House the ideal, which is ours, we of the Ralliement Credi-tiste. I urge the members of all other parties who are willing to share it to follow the example of the Liberal member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan) and to resign from their party in order to freely express their opinions. Provided they have the same courage, they should, with the help of the former Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), join the ranks of free people like us, as we have no financial ties and no election funds to dictate our policy. Let them consider seriously the proposals we are making today and let them not hesitate to join us, so that all people of goodwill may join together to have justice done.
In order to show that even the government sometimes understands this problem, I should like to quote the statements made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), in San Francisco, on December 1 last and I quote:
Few problems are more disturbing than that of permanent and oppressive poverty. That such poverty should exist in Canada, as shown in the report of our Economic Council, is a disgrace.
The Minister of Justice added the following:
It is useless to explain the nature of poverty to the poor, they know it quite well. They feel helplessness and despair as wounds, and destitution, as frustrations. They know what it means to live in dilapidated houses, to have no other park than the cracked street pavement and no other animal life than the rodents infesting their home. No task force impression is more vivid of mind and depressing of spirit than those formed amid the blight and slum of Canada's larger cities.
In the most dilapidated downtown areas; ... poverty stares you in the face. It can be seen, heard, tasted, felt.
The poor know what it is to live tossed about by sickness, family quarrels, interrupted studies and chronic unemployment. They know what it is to be victims of debts, discouragement, bondage and delinquency.
The first physical need of the poor is that of decent lodging. Goodwill goes to waste in yards littered with rubbish, half-torn walls, gaping windows, cold radiators and drippy ceilings. The poor live in slums, and the slums make new poor.

DEBATES	December 9, 1969
If the Minister of Justice can make such statements and yet, in cabinet, cannot make himself heard, he can see the destitution even though he finds no solution. As early as tomorrow, he should recommend the study of the motion we have moved to the cabinet, so that, once and for all, all economic problems can be solved; and the shameless destitution be done away with; for if we can reach the moon, we can also feed humanity.
I agree with him: let us allow every family head to have a home of his own. But this cannot be done at interest rates of 10 and 11 per cent, such as we now have. Our minister can come out with those statements, but I wonder if he has spoken to the house of the paralysis of the Canadian economy.
Unfortunately, we notice that, the problem exists but when the time comes to correct it, we do not have the courage to denounce the financial sharks. The government is not firm enough.
So, here is what we advocate. I want to define clearly that we propose in order to help building up a country that belongs to the Canadians.
Everybody understands now that it is certainly not by lending money at an interest rate of 11 per cent or more, that we are going to save Canada.
Indeed, it is not by lending money to farmers at an interest rate of 9 per cent that we are going to help the agricultural class. It is not by letting the municipalities borrow money in Germany that we are going to solve the problem of inflation. It is not by allowing Quebec Hydro to borrow money on the American market at an interest rate of 11 per cent that we will reduce the cost of living, because already the province of Quebec, which is in serious financial situation, finds it difficult to borrow money. Let us refer, in this regard, to the requests of Premier Bertrand. Finally, it is not by imposing new taxes as it is intended for 1971, particularly on capital gains, that we will encourage Canadians to invest in Canada.
Let me analyse the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) concerning the taxing of capital gains. I think it is unsafe and, in my opinion, it will discourage private enterprise. Besides, I will give only one example to show how the government is ready to enforce an unjust legislation.
If an individual purchased bonds in 1965 at $5 each, when taxing him on capital gains they will decide to take as a basis the present lower market prices.
December 9, 19G9
Those shares may be worth $3 today, but if, as is quite probable, prices resume their upward trend in 1974 or 1975, the Minister of Finance will be collecting taxes on a loss of $2 per share.
So I feel that the act is unfair. That is why I urge the Minister of Finance to reshape it in order to avoid inequities, because all those who invested their money in Canadian companies will otherwise invest it in American companies, which would lead to a drain of Canadian capital to o her countries as our Canadian economy is stifled by the Minister of Finance who fails to pay heed to the voice of reason, or if you like to that of Creditistes.
Having said this, I should like to explain above all what Creditistes are suggesting to revive the Canadian economy which is on the brink of self-destruction while politicians are unable to give it a new stimulus in order to bring it back to life.
Our economy is gnawed by the cancer of inflation; it needs a new heart. Why not put new life into the dying through a Creditiste transplant?
Mr. Speaker, what I want to define now is, first, the objective of economic activity in any country, and essentially this objective is that the economy must meet human needs. As we understand it, under the present system, people have to live in misery and austerity, despite the present and potential affluence which could make it possible to meet all those human needs.
When studying the present monetary system and its effects, one notes that the major cause of disorder derives mainly, if not solely, from the fact that the consumers do not have enough money.
To confirm the statements of social credit supporters, let us remember those words that the great international financier, Vincent Cartwright Vickers, governor of the Bank of England, said in 1939, before dying, and I quote:
With the help of nature, man is now able to produce more than he can consume, more food than he can eat, more clothing than he can wear, more housing than he needs.
If producers can increase their production, if ships, railways and other means of transportation are waiting to carry the resources and to provide the services they have to offer, the fault must lie with the consumer. Why does the latter paralyse trade, industry and world progress, and why does he prevent the advent of a durable peace by deliberately refusing all the good things that the world
Monetary Proposals of Social Credit Party puts at his disposal? The answer is obvious. The consumer cannot afford to buy more because he does not have enough money. Unless one is prejudiced, the only possible conclusion is that the health and welfare of the individual, the happiness of the community and world peace depend mostly if not entirely on the monetary problem.
Of the amounts that business concerns transfer to the consumers, only a part is distributed to them, as revenue, as a payment for their services. The rest is transferred to other businesses as a payment for raw materials and equipment. As a result, the purchasing power of individuals does not enable them to buy the entire production. This theory has been criticized and not without some unfairness. The sums paid to other businesses, as has been noted, finally result in the distribution of income, since these other businesses also have to pay the services of the production factors used by them. This is undoubtedly true, but the payments as a whole are made only after an extremely long delay. This means that the purchasing power distributed in the course of production is never enough to buy the entire production whose value would keep on increasing. Douglas's thesis would therefore be valid on the "dynamic" plan.
"It would be true to say that the national income would be equal to the national production", writes Douglas, "if all wages, salaries and dividends related to production were used at the very moment they have been earned so as to purchase the production that distributed them." But such is not the case and over the gap between production and distribution is erected a mass of on credit buying power which never appears as income.
And so, the solution would be to adjust the global buying power to the global amount of the production prices. The Social Credit proposes to make this adjustment of the buying power necessary to the purchasing of the whole production and to the satisfaction of the consumers' needs in so far as the national economy permits by distributing a national dividend to each and every citizen, and by adjusting periodically the prices to the current buying power, so as to stop inflation.
A national dividend paid periodically to every citizen and the compensated discount are the two aspects of the plan for the distribution of wealth and services proposed by the supporters of Social Credit.
Credit is synonymous with trust. Credit is given to a trustworthy person. The physician

December 9, 1969
1762	COMMONS
Monetary Proposals of Social Credit Party will enjoy the esteem of his patients and will have credit with them if they feel he can give them the care required by their condition. The pioneers who settled in America were confident that the new world would provide them with the necessities of life. That was the actual credit of America.
Many industries are starting everywhere, even in desert regions of northern Quebec. People trust to the future of Quebec and of Canada. That is the actual credit of the province of Quebec and of Canada.
The measure of the actual credit of a country, a province or a business resides in the exact evaluation of its capacity to produce and deliver the goods in sufficient quantity at the right place and at the time required by prospective consumers. More specifically, the actual credit of the wealth of a country or a province can be expressed in terms of potential goods and services.
One realizes then that the actual credit is made up of two factors: the capacity to produce and the requirements to be met. Both factors are closely related. The producer of wealth that nobody wants is as useless as a consumer of goods which are not produced. The consumer is as necessary to the production of actual credit as the producer. Actual credit is a joint creation.
Not only is the consumer as essential as the producer to create actual credit but the community as a whole is even more essential. From the economic point of view, a nation is an association of people engaged in the production of actual credit and thus, the government, as the guardian of actual credit of the community, must also protect the interests of both producers and consumers, since both are equally essential to the creation of actual credit.
However, since producers and consumers form together the whole community, we can conclude that actual credit has a social or joint origin: it belongs neither to the producer nor to the consumer, but jointly to the community of which everyone is a part.
Therefore, actual credit is a social factor. It is common and social, because it is the basis of the entire community. It derives its efficiency from the producers and the consumers; from the producers, acting as suppliers of capital and entrepreneurs, as well as the producers working with their own hands and their brains for the common task of developing the country and the whole world.


On the other hand, the other basis consists of the consumers. For instance, we know that a shoe factory would not be worth anything if the users of shoes decided to go barefoot, in the same way as a refrigerator factory is unthinkable at the North Pole, because there are no consumers, no buyers of that product in that area.
Therefore, we may conclude that Social Credit, far from being only a theory, is an undeniable fact.
That is why Tudor Jones who succeeded Major Douglas as chairman of the Social Credit secretariat, defined Social Credit as follows:
The ability of human beings living in a society to attain the desired ends to their satisfaction.

speechtext:
Perhaps not, but to the end I will say that it is never too late to take a step in the right direction and there will always be time for approval.
The difference between actual credit and financial credit is that actual credit is based upon things, tangible goods actual or potential, whereas financial credit is based on money which, as we know, often bears no relation to things and produced wealth.
But it is clear however that financial credit based on money should reflect real credit, since money has value only if it allows to obtain things and wealth as well as to meet basic needs.
We are therefore finding out that financial credit serves to activate and to orient real credit. We know that money allows plants to operate, machines to run and workers to produce.
The banker finances the shoe manufacturer's real credit. He lends him money on
December 9, 1969

one condition only, that it be reimbursed to the bank not with shoes but with more money than was borrowed.
Here we have then the eventual consumers.
If there are no potential consumers or very few of them, the bank will make no loans at all or only a few. Financial credit is issued by the banks not to the producers of wealth considered as such, but to the producers of wealth considered also as producers of money.
As Major Douglas said: If a producer succeeds in convincing a bank that if he produces less, in other words, that in reducing production he will achieve a monopolistic position, he will certainly get a loan. One realizes that the banker is not interested in meeting the consumers' needs but rather in getting his money back with interests.
Meanwhile, we, the supporters of Social Credit and actual credit, believe that our credit is based on tangible things, on certainties, that it originates, so to speak, from the Creator's kindness, who put into earth, water and air all the resources necessary to satisfy people, and provided them with two arms, a mind and brains to make use of such wealth.
Financial credit, which should reflect actual credit, has been created by men, individuals, private organizations that can control and restrict it as they wish and can arbitrarily call for tight money during times when credit should be expanded.
In order to play its role as generator, financial credit must reflect actual credit, mesh with economic factors and consumers' needs. As Douglas said, a modern and efficient financial system should aim at expanding the consumer's credit to the limit of his capacity to produce.
What to do then? As Douglas said, provide additional purchasing power not included in the price of manufactured goods, thus stabilizing prices and enabling consumers to regain control over production.
According to Major Douglas, the price of an item with regard to its production cost, should bear the same relationship as does the production of the actual item with regard to the national consumption. Thus if an item costs $4, the consumer should be able to secure it for $3. That is the explanation of the compensated discount.
Social Credit therefore suggests to allow consumers to grant an additional purchasing power equal to the difference between production and consumption, or to decrease the
Monetary Proposals of Social Credit Party production price to the actual cost which is that of consumption. In the first instance, it is a matter of dividend; in the other, it is a matter of compensated discount.
We have therefore proved that actual credit is social credit, a common credit, a credit shared by everyone.
In 1934, Major Douglas testified before members of the Standing Committee on Banking and Credit. When questioned as to the source of the national dividend, he replied:
The origin of the national dividend can be explained in two ways: first by a very simply stated sentence, which is a matter of importance nowadays, a predominant factor. That is what happens, for example, when ten men are pulling a load. If each man draws on his own, they could exert their efforts for a whole week without moving the load at all, but if the ten of them take a rope and pull together, the thing comes off easily. It cannot be said that the huge increase in production made possible because of the partnership is the result of the particular efforts of one person; it comes from the group as a whole.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, we are convinced, in introducing this motion, that we are doing a service to Canadians, since we ask them to help us get rid of the tax burden and forget it altogether. Let us keep on making suggestions as we have done lately, by saying: Let us forget railroad taxes, old war debts, and let us rather build a country on the credit that we know is real, on the capabilities of the machines and the brains at our disposal. By calling upon all men of good will, since there is no shortage of products in Canada, everybody will have a home and will be happy to live in Canada, and the federal-provincial feuds of today would vanish into thin air.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to take part in this debate because there have been so many conflicting viewpoints expressed. I wish to say right off the bat that many things have been said here this afternoon with which I do not agree. The last speaker, and the Creditiste members who have spoken, have treated the motion most sincerely.
What the motion is really asking us to do is to give everyone in Canada a dividend by printing more money. It suggests the Bank of Canada should give everybody a $1,000 bill or $1,000 credit which they can spend. In this way, those unfortunate people who do not have an electric stove, new car, or whatever they are lacking could buy what they want.
1764	COMMONS
Monetary Proposals of Social Credit Party There is just one flaw in this proposal. I am sure ail Canadian citizens would be glad to accept this money, but I wonder how the rest of the world would look upon it? This course has been followed on numerous occasions throughout history. I ask my very sincere friends in the Creditiste movement to read the history of Germany. Following World War I, that country printed money as if it were going completely out of style. As a result, their money became worthless. The same thing has happened to a lesser extent in Italy since World War II. That country has devalued its money at least six times, and maybe more. A short while ago France devalued its money for the second or third time since World War II.
I suggest if Canada starts printing money its dollar will be less valuable. Instead of our dollar being worth 93 cents in United States currency, it would only be worth 65 cents or 75 cents. We would lose the confidence of the financial people of the world. That is what would happen. When we would purchase goods from a foreign land, they would cost us much more. It is as simple as that. Instead of our dollar being worth 93 cents when purchasing grapefruit from California or Florida, it would only be worth 65 cents or 75 cents.
While this situation might be of benefit to the citizens of Canada in the immediate future-for about ten minutes I suggest-as soon as the financial people of the world heard about it our dollar would be devalued and they would have no confidence in the money of Canada. That is a fact, my friends, and there is no way you can argue around it. The Creditiste members are very sincere, so I hesitate to go as far as I might in saying these things. They remind me of a little girl six or eight years of age who listens with great interest when we tell her the story of Cinderella or Jack and the Beanstalk. Of course, the little girl believes it. These members also believe a fairy story. I suggest they should read about some of the things that have happened in the world in years gone by. Printing money simply does not work. It has not worked in Canada and, frankly, in the past few years we have been printing money-not $1,000 bills, but $1,000 bonds. We had been going in debt each and every year up to the moment that this great government took office. Consequently, we have this inflationary period. Money is not as valuable as it was previously because we have printed too much of it. If we print any more, it will be of less value than it is now.

DEBATES	December 9, 1969
One of the participants in the debate, I forget which one, mentioned that this inflationary period is worse than the depression and, therefore, we must do something about it. I believe it was a Creditiste member who suggested we should give a national dividend. This suggestion is also made in the second paragraph of the motion. This inflationary period cannot be underemphasized. It is a terrible thing. It is really legalized robbery, that is what it is. A small businessman or farmer who retired 15 years ago with $50,000 in bonds or cash in the bank, and who has been fortunate enough to live for the past 15 years, finds that today his $50,000 is worth only $25,000. That is what I call legalized robbery. The government must do something about inflation. I hope the steps they are taking are sufficient. If not, something further must be done. I do not hesitate to agree with our government officials, our high priced help behind the curtains, who state that something that works in wartime will not necessarily work in peacetime. I agree with that.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
But something must be done, and it may be that prices wages and profits should be pegged as they were during the last war and in other wars. Let me emphasize this, however: while inflation today is terrible, let no one think it is as bad as it was back in the 'thirties. How many homes in Canada today lack a refrigerator or electric stove? How many do not possess a radio? How many have not one, but two cars? While I have every sympathy with the poor, the fact is that the poor today are not as poor as they were yesterday and that we in Canada can stand to attention before the rest of the world and say that within reason we have done a good job. I repeat what was said by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert)-the sympathy we have for our fellow human beings who are less well off or less fortunate than we are, is not limited to members of one party.
If you do not believe me, Mr. Speaker, when I say we have done reasonably well, ask those hon. members on your left which other country in the world they would prefer. Would it be Italy or France, or Russia or China? Sometimes when I hear hon. members over there, members who are not all the way to the left, asking silly questions about Russia and China, and telling us what terrible things our friends to the south are doing, I think it might be a good idea if they were to take a slow boat to China and find out how living
December 9, 1969

conditions are there. I say we can hold our heads up reasonably well in this old world. Of course there is poverty in this country of ours but over the last 25 years Canada has done a very great deal to lessen its effects. Let us remind ourselves of such things as disability pensions. Do these exist in countries all over the world? What about such things as blind persons' pensions and old age pensions? Everyone in this chamber believes old age pensions should be increased. But how many dollars a month did our grandfathers get as old age pensioners in Canada? They did not get anything at all unless they have died just lately.
We have done a reasonable job. It is true our old age pensioners need more money, but suppose we doubled the present pension from, say, $109 a month to $218 a month. It would cost us $1,400,000,000. Hon. members in the far corner suggest we should print a little money and give it to the pensioners that way. But what would be the point of printing money if next morning the dollar was worth only 50 cents?
One way in which we can improve the lot of our citizens is by hard work. This has been proved in a country like Germany; it has been proved in Japan. It is unfortunate, remembering the awful wan- we fought, that the only country Germany is jealous of today is the other country which lost the war, namely, Japan. The reason is that over there people have a great desire to do all the work they can. To the hon. members who support this motion I make the following suggestion: they should take a trip to Germany or Japan and watch the people there going to work. They do not walk to work; they run to work. They see not how little they can do, but how much. This is why only a month ago the German Deutschmark was revalued upward and made more valuable.
There are other things we can be proud of here, such as the mothers' allowance. The amount could be increased, of course. Who would not be sympathetic to a situation of a deserving mother with three or four children to bring up. We know that in some of the provinces the money provided is not sufficient. Nevertheless, it is a lot more that it was 25 years ago and it will buy a great deal more, too. Take unemployment insurance. This is something which many hon. members feel has been abused. I, too, believe abuses have taken place on many occasions. Nevertheless, its introduction represented a great step forward. Who in this chamber would suggest that veterans do not deserve more
Monetary Proposals of Social Credit Party money, especially those who gave their all so you and I might have an opportunity to speak as we see fit in this chamber? At the same time, who will say that our veterans are not treated better than any in the whole world today? And after legislation has been presented and dealt with here in the House of Commons in the course of the next few months I am sure the benefits available to them will be even greater.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) delivered quite an oration on the subject of the poor. It would have been much more applicable in Biblical times when they really had poor people. He seems to feel there is no sympathy in the hearts of supporters of the government for those who are on the brink of what is described as poverty. All of us are in erested in their situation. The hon. member went on to suggest that simply because a man is a Canadian he should have the right to get a cheque every month from the government- not because he is disabled, not because he is blind, not because he is old, not because he is sick, but because he is here. Mr. Speaker, you will never shove that down my throat. While the Government of Canada has an obligation to provide us with a chance to make a living, it does not have any obligation to provide us with a living.
You and I, as citizens of Canada, have some
obligations, too. One of them, if we have the ability and the required capacity, is to go to work. Work is a four-letter word which in the case of a small minority, a small percentage of Canadians, particularly among some of our young people, is not as well known as other four-letter words. I suggest that special attention be paid all over Canada to this word "work", spelled w-o-r-k. It is very necessary. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre maintains that he, as a Canadian, should get a cheque every month from the treasury of Canada without necessarily doing any work. In suggesting that, I believe he is like one of the three blind mice, going round in a circle continually without knowing when to stop. Indeed, it amazes me that a man like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, one who is unquestionably sincere, one who knows more about this parliament than I shall ever know, should be unaware of the fact that in the world today socialism, giving something away for nothing, simply will not work. Let him look over to England, that once mighty country which only a few decades ago practically ran the world but which today is

Monetary Proposals of Social Credit Party drowning in a sea of socialism. If socialism is such a wonderful thing, if we should all get a cheque each month for the privilege of being Canadian, why is there no provision made on those lines in the United States, the country whose people enjoy by far the highest standard of living in the world?
There are many things we can complain about when we think of our United States friends. It is true that in many ways they have not done too well. But one thing in respect of which they cannot be criticized is the standard of living enjoyed in that country. It is the highest in the world, and it was achieved without what I call-and, to me, this is a horrible word-socialism.
How can we help our poor who are living on the brink of poverty, Mr. Speaker? I say we shall do it by educating them, and we are educating them. Today there are more of our children than ever going to universities and trade schools. They will be better citizens, equipped to go into the world and make a living.
